title: OpenClaw vs Hermes Agent: where Metal fits
h1: openclaw vs hermes agent: which one should you run?
description: Compare OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and Metal on setup, agent teams, scheduling and hosting, with dated sources and no performance rankings.
answer: **choose who handles the upkeep before choosing the agent.** openclaw and hermes can run on your machine or server. openclaw centres on chat channels and routing. hermes adds persistent memory and self-created skills.[^1][^3] both give you open-source code to change. dusk puts named bots with separate jobs in an app, with hosting available when you want it.
og_line: two open agents, a third way to work.

them: **you want code you can change.** both openclaw and hermes use the mit license.
**you want agents through chat apps.** compare openclaw's message routing with hermes' isolated subagents.
dusk: **you want visible teammates.** each named bot keeps its own job, chats and memory.
**you want dusk to host the machine.** move the bots when overnight work starts to matter.

compare.h: three ways to keep an agent running
compare.intro: **pick the setup you want to live with every day.** as of 12 november 2026, hermes offers its own agent and hosting options. dusk is a separate app, not an open-source fork of either project.

method:
**try the same small job before moving your work.** Metal is based on Dusk Bot. this comparison uses product sources checked on 12 november 2026 and dusk docs.

we have not run head-to-head tasks or measured installation times. we leave out security rankings because disclosure counts cannot rank safety. the rows compare setup and features, not answer quality.

sections.h: start where you want to talk
sections.md:
**start in the chat app you actually want to use.** openclaw and hermes both list whatsapp and telegram.[^1][^3] a desktop screenshot tells you little about that fit.

openclaw routes conversations to isolated agents through rules it calls bindings.[^5] hermes gives subagents their own conversations and terminals.[^3] compare the handoff you need. [openclaw vs dusk](/vs/openclaw) looks closer at that route.

sections.h: put the files where the agent runs
sections.md:
**the job needs its files after the installer finishes.** decide where the work and source material should live.

- both open projects can run on your server; paid nous portal plans also include a hermes cloud agent.[^1][^3]
- both have desktop or terminal paths. don't assume openclaw needs docker or hermes needs a terminal.[^2][^4]
- connect the model and read the terms for that exact use.
- try a small job, such as comparing two files, before giving it sensitive material.

if neither setup fits, see [hermes alternatives](/alternatives/hermes-agent).

sections.h: choose a group when you want to join the conversation
sections.md:
**visible roles help you follow the handoff.** in dusk, one bot can read a brief while another questions its assumptions.

choose only when mentioned to control replies, or leader to have one bot hand out work. each keeps its own ai and permissions.[^8] use a group when you want to question the handoff yourself.

the [group chat guide](/ai-group-chat) covers those choices. recurring reviews still need an awake machine with dusk open. use dusk cloud when they must run while your computer sleeps.[^10]

faq.q: did anyone create a group chat of agents?
faq.a: **yes. choose whether you want to join in.** dusk has shared threads, mentions and a leader.[^8] openclaw lists isolated agents and group-chat use; hermes lists subagents.[^5][^3] choose between joining the conversation and handing work away.

faq.q: where do your agents actually run when your laptop is closed?
faq.a: **somewhere that stays on.** openclaw supports your server. hermes supports your server or a paid nous portal cloud agent.[^1][^3] dusk cloud hosts your dusk bots' machine.[^7]

faq.q: is hermes agent paid or free?
faq.a: **the mit software is free.** as of 12 november 2026, nous portal has a free tier and paid plans from $20 monthly. your model and hosting choices shape the ongoing cost.[^3]
